ba-w1-q1.question: A subscription video app's main goal is to grow next quarter's subscription revenue. Which of these is a **leading** indicator?
options: Total subscription revenue of the last quarter
Number of free trials started this week
Number of subscribers who cancelled last month
Net profit of the last financial year
ba-w1-q1.explanation: Free trials start today and convert into paid subscriptions a few weeks later, so they signal future revenue in advance: option B is a leading indicator. Trap: option C (last month's cancellations) also looks like 'customer behaviour', but it is an outcome that has already happened, i.e. lagging; options A and D are lagging financial results too.

ba-w1-q2.question: A D2C brand's website had 1,60,000 sessions, 4,000 orders and ₹18,00,000 revenue in a month. What are the conversion rate (orders / sessions) and the AOV?
options: Conversion 4%, AOV ₹450
Conversion 2.5%, AOV ₹11.25
Conversion 40%, AOV ₹4,500
Conversion 2.5%, AOV ₹450
ba-w1-q2.explanation: Conversion = 4,000 / 1,60,000 = 0.025 = 2.5%. AOV = revenue / orders = 18,00,000 / 4,000 = ₹450, so option D is correct. Trap: option B divides revenue by sessions (₹11.25 is revenue per session, not AOV); options A and C misplace a decimal or a zero.

ba-w1-q3.question: One day's data for three stores of a retail chain: Store P: 50 purchases / 1,000 visitors, Store Q: 30 / 200, Store R: 20 / 800. What is the chain's overall visitor-to-purchase conversion?
ba-w1-q3.explanation: Overall = Σ purchases / Σ visitors = (50 + 30 + 20) / (1,000 + 200 + 800) = 100 / 2,000 = 5.0%, i.e. option A. Trap: option B is the simple average of the three store rates (5%, 15%, 2.5%), which gives the small Store Q as much weight as the big stores; options C and D are just one store's rate.

ba-w1-q4.question: A dashboard bar chart shows a customer satisfaction score of 92 for Brand X and 94 for Brand Y, but the y-axis starts at 90. How much longer does Y's bar look than X's, and what is the real difference?
options: About 2.2% longer, both visually and in reality
Visually 2.2% longer, in reality 2 times
Visually 2 times as long, in reality only about 2.2% higher
Visually 4 times as long, in reality 2 points higher
ba-w1-q4.explanation: The axis starts at 90, so the bar heights are 92 − 90 = 2 and 94 − 90 = 4 units: Y's bar looks 2 times as long. The real ratio is 94 / 92 = 1.022, i.e. only about 2.2% higher, so option C. Trap: option D treats 4 as the ratio (4 is just the height of Y's bar); option A would be right only if the axis started at 0.

ba-w1-q5.question: A customer-support team's new KPI is 'tickets closed per agent per day', and a bonus is tied to it. In two months the KPI rose 40%, but complaints rose too. Which guardrail metric best catches this problem?
options: Percentage of tickets reopened within 7 days
Total login hours of each agent
Number of new tickets arriving each day
Average time taken to close a ticket
ba-w1-q5.explanation: Because of the bonus, agents can close tickets without solving them (Goodhart's law). The reopen rate (option A) directly checks whether a closed ticket was really resolved, so it is the right guardrail. Trap: option D (average handle time) also sounds quality-related, but rushing tickets closed makes it look even 'better', so it does not catch the gaming; options B and C measure effort and demand, not quality.

ba-w1-q6.question: An e-commerce site's revenue = sessions × conversion rate × AOV. Next month sessions are expected to fall 4% and AOV will stay the same. By roughly how much (relative %) must the conversion rate rise for revenue to grow 10%?
ba-w1-q6.explanation: The factors multiply: 0.96 × (1 + g) × 1 = 1.10, so 1 + g = 1.10 / 0.96 = 1.1458, i.e. g ≈ 14.6%, option C. Trap: option A adds the percentages (10 + 4 = 14%), which is wrong in a multiplicative tree; option B (10 − 4) also flips the sign, and option D ignores the fall in sessions.

ba-w2-q1.question: A fashion e-tailer's return rate rose from 8% to 10% this quarter. How is this change described correctly?
options: 2 percentage points, which is also a 2% relative increase
An increase of 25 percentage points
An increase of 2 percentage points, i.e. a 25% relative increase
An increase of 10 percentage points, i.e. a 125% relative increase
ba-w2-q1.explanation: Absolute change = 10 − 8 = 2 percentage points; relative change = 2 / 8 = 0.25 = 25%, so option C. Trap: option A treats pp and relative % as the same (2 pp is a 25% relative change, not 2%); option B writes the relative 25% as percentage points by mistake.

ba-w2-q2.question: In a loyalty programme, 300 Gold members spend ₹800 per month on average and 700 Silver members spend ₹400. What is the average monthly spend of all 1,000 members?
ba-w2-q2.explanation: Weighted average = (300 × 800 + 700 × 400) / 1,000 = (2,40,000 + 2,80,000) / 1,000 = ₹520, i.e. option A. Trap: option B is the simple average of the two segment averages, which underweights the larger Silver segment; option C swaps the weights (0.7 × 800 + 0.3 × 400); option D adds the two averages.

ba-w2-q3.question: Lead conversions of two sales reps (fictional data): Asha: warm leads 45 / 60, cold leads 12 / 140. Bilal: warm leads 120 / 180, cold leads 1 / 20. Which statement is correct?
options: Bilal beats Asha in both lead types, so he is ahead overall too
Asha is ahead overall and in both lead types, in all three
Both have equal overall conversion because both have 200 leads
Asha is better in each lead type, but Bilal is ahead overall because 90% of his leads are warm
ba-w2-q3.explanation: Asha: warm 75%, cold 8.6%, overall 57 / 200 = 28.5%. Bilal: warm 66.7%, cold 5%, overall 121 / 200 = 60.5%. Asha leads in every segment, but Bilal got 180 / 200 = 90% warm (easy) leads, so Bilal is ahead overall: option D (Simpson's paradox). Trap: option A looks only at the overall number and assumes Bilal is better everywhere; option C confuses equal lead counts with equal conversion.

ba-w2-q4.question: Orders of a food brand (fictional): last year App 600 orders with AOV ₹500, Web 400 orders with AOV ₹900. This year App 1,500 orders with AOV ₹520, Web 500 orders with AOV ₹950. What is this year's overall AOV, and what happened compared with last year's ₹660?
options: ₹692; both channels' AOV rose, so the overall rose too
₹627.50; both channels' AOV rose, yet the overall fell because the mix shifted towards the cheaper App
₹735; the overall AOV rose
₹660; the overall AOV stayed the same
ba-w2-q4.explanation: This year's overall = (1,500 × 520 + 500 × 950) / 2,000 = (7,80,000 + 4,75,000) / 2,000 = ₹627.50, which is below ₹660. App's share went from 60% to 75%: the mix effect overpowered the rate effect, so option B. Trap: option A uses last year's 60:40 mix (0.6 × 520 + 0.4 × 950 = 692); option C is the simple average of the two AOVs.

ba-w2-q5.question: A SaaS company has 1,000 customers: North has 120 Premium + 280 Basic, South has 80 Premium + 520 Basic. The board asks: 'What % of Premium customers are from the North?'
ba-w2-q5.explanation: The question's denominator is the Premium column total: 120 + 80 = 200. North Premium = 120, so 120 / 200 = 60%, option A. Trap: option B is the row % (120 of North's 400 customers = 30% are Premium), which answers the reverse question; option C is the total % (120 / 1,000); option D is the South's share.

ba-w2-q6.question: Two discount strategies (fictional) were tested in different stores. Strategy P: 30% redemption in urban stores (900 customers), 10% in rural (100 customers). Strategy Q: urban 32% (200 customers), rural 12% (800 customers). After standardising to the combined customer mix (urban 1,100, rural 900), which strategy is better and by how many percentage points?
options: P, by 12 percentage points
Q, by 2 percentage points
They are equal
Q, by 4 percentage points
ba-w2-q6.explanation: Common mix: urban 1,100 / 2,000 = 0.55, rural 0.45. P = 0.55 × 30 + 0.45 × 10 = 21%; Q = 0.55 × 32 + 0.45 × 12 = 23%. Q is better by 2 pp, option B. Trap: option A compares the crude overall rates (P 28%, Q 16%), which are biased by P's urban-heavy mix; option D adds the two segment gaps (2 + 2).

ba-w3-q1.question: A beverage company runs a chi-square test of independence on a contingency table of 4 cities and 3 brands. How many degrees of freedom does the test have?
ba-w3-q1.explanation: df = (r − 1)(c − 1) = (4 − 1)(3 − 1) = 3 × 2 = 6, option A. Trap: option B is the number of cells (4 × 3), and option C is cells − 1, which is the goodness-of-fit formula, not independence; option D adds (4 − 1) + (3 − 1).

ba-w3-q2.question: A survey table of 3 cities × 4 brands has N = 400. Kolkata's row total is 120 and Brand B's column total is 150. Under independence, what is the expected count of the (Kolkata, Brand B) cell?
ba-w3-q2.explanation: E = row total × column total / N = 120 × 150 / 400 = 45, option C. Trap: option A (120 / 4) assumes all four brands are equally popular, which H₀ does not say; H₀ only says Kolkata's brand mix equals the overall mix. Option B (150 / 4) and option D (150 × 150 / 400) use the wrong totals.

ba-w3-q3.question: Of 100 Delhi customers, 60 prefer Brand X and 40 prefer Brand Y; of 100 Mumbai customers, 45 prefer X and 55 prefer Y. Which is the correct result of a chi-square test of independence without continuity correction (α = 0.05; critical values: 3.841 at df = 1, 5.991 at df = 2)?
options: χ² ≈ 2.26, H₀ is not rejected
χ² ≈ 4.51, reject H₀: brand preference and city are associated
χ² ≈ 4.51, H₀ is not rejected because 4.51 < 5.991
χ² ≈ 4.51, and this proves that city causes brand preference
ba-w3-q3.explanation: Column totals X = 105, Y = 95; each row 100, N = 200. E = 52.5 (X) and 47.5 (Y) in both rows. Every cell has |O − E| = 7.5, so χ² = 7.5² × (1/52.5 + 1/47.5) × 2 ≈ 4.51. df = 1, 4.51 > 3.841 ⇒ reject, option B. Trap: option C uses the df = 2 critical value (a 2×2 table has df = 1); option A adds only one row's cells; option D turns association into causation.

ba-w3-q4.question: Below are the observed (O) and expected (E) counts of four cells from a significant chi-square test (3×4 table). Which cell contributes the most to χ²?
options: Mumbai–Brand P: O = 130, E = 115
Delhi–Brand R: O = 48, E = 40
Jaipur–Brand Q: O = 12, E = 20
Lucknow–Brand S: O = 25, E = 15
ba-w3-q4.explanation: Contribution = (O − E)² / E: option A 225 / 115 ≈ 1.96, option B 64 / 40 = 1.6, option C 64 / 20 = 3.2, option D 100 / 15 ≈ 6.67. The largest is option D. Trap: option A has the largest |O − E| = 15, but dividing by a large E makes its contribution small; χ² measures the gap relative to the expected count, not the absolute gap.

ba-w3-q5.question: A 3 × 4 table of 300 customers (3 income bands × 4 brands) gives χ² = 24. What is Cramér's V?
ba-w3-q5.explanation: k = min(3, 4) = 3, so V = √(χ² / (N(k − 1))) = √(24 / (300 × 2)) = √0.04 = 0.20, option C. Trap: option A forgets the square root; option B forgets (k − 1) and takes √(24 / 300); option D uses k = 3 instead of k − 1.

ba-w3-q6.question: Survey 1: Delhi (100) has 55 X / 45 Y, Mumbai (100) has 45 X / 55 Y. In Survey 2 every cell is 4 times larger: Delhi 220 / 180, Mumbai 180 / 220. The 5% critical value at df = 1 is 3.841. Which statement is correct?
options: Survey 1 has χ² = 2.0 (not significant), Survey 2 has χ² = 8.0 (significant), but φ (Cramér's V) is 0.1 in both
Both surveys have χ² = 2.0 because the proportions are the same
In Survey 2, χ² = 8.0 and φ also grew 4 times to 0.4, i.e. a strong association
In Survey 2, χ² = 4.0 (√4 = 2 times), significant
ba-w3-q6.explanation: Survey 1: E = 50 in every cell, χ² = 4 × 5² / 50 = 2.0 < 3.841. Survey 2: E = 200, χ² = 4 × 20² / 200 = 8.0 > 3.841. φ = √(χ² / N) = √(2 / 200) = √(8 / 800) = 0.1 in both, so option A. Trap: option C assumes the effect size grows with N; χ² grew because the evidence grew, while the strength of association is unchanged. Option B forgets that χ² depends on counts.

ba-w4-q1.question: An analyst runs 3 pairwise t-tests, each at α = 0.05, to compare the average bill of 3 store formats. If the tests are treated as independent and there is in fact no difference, what is the probability of at least one false positive?
options: About 14.3%
ba-w4-q1.explanation: FWER = 1 − (1 − 0.05)³ = 1 − 0.857375 ≈ 0.143, i.e. about 14.3%, option D. Trap: option B adds 3 × 0.05; that is only an upper bound (Bonferroni inequality), not the exact probability. Option A assumes each test's 5% stays 5% for the whole analysis.

ba-w4-q2.question: A company compares the sales lift of 4 ad campaigns; each campaign ran in 5 different stores (20 stores in total). What are the degrees of freedom of the one-way ANOVA F-statistic?
ba-w4-q2.explanation: Between-groups df = k − 1 = 4 − 1 = 3; within-groups df = N − k = 20 − 4 = 16, so F(3, 16), option B. Trap: option C uses the total df (N − 1 = 19) as the within df; options A and D take the number of groups itself as the df.

ba-w4-q3.question: 4 pricing plans with 10 customers each (N = 40). The ANOVA gives SSB = 120 and SSW = 360. The 5% critical value of F(3, 36) is 2.866. What is the correct conclusion?
options: F ≈ 0.33, H₀ is not rejected
F = 12.0, reject H₀
F = 4.0, reject H₀: at least one plan's mean differs from the others
F = 4.0, reject H₀: all four plans' means differ from each other
ba-w4-q3.explanation: MSB = 120 / 3 = 40, MSW = 360 / 36 = 10, F = 40 / 10 = 4.0 > 2.866, so reject; ANOVA only says that at least one mean differs, so option C. Trap: option D has the same F but stretches the conclusion; which pairs differ is for a post-hoc test. Option B forgets to divide SSB by its df (120 / 10), and option A takes SSB / SSW.

ba-w4-q4.question: A checkout-page A/B test: version A got 120 orders from 2,000 visitors, version B got 150 orders from 2,000 visitors. What is the correct result of a pooled two-proportion z-test (two-sided, α = 0.05, critical value 1.96)?
options: z ≈ 1.89; not significant at the 5% two-sided level
z ≈ 1.89; significant, because the relative lift is 25%
z ≈ 2.67; significant
z ≈ 1.89; significant, because 1.89 > 1.645
ba-w4-q4.explanation: p̂_A = 0.06, p̂_B = 0.075, pooled p̂ = 270 / 4,000 = 0.0675. SE = √(0.0675 × 0.9325 × (1/2,000 + 1/2,000)) ≈ 0.00793. z = 0.015 / 0.00793 ≈ 1.89 < 1.96, so option A. Trap: option D uses the one-sided critical value (1.645) although the test was fixed as two-sided; option C uses only one 1/n in the SE; option B mistakes the size of the lift for significance.

ba-w4-q5.question: An ANOVA of 4 delivery partners gives a significant F. Now all pairwise comparisons are to be done with a Bonferroni correction, family-wise α = 0.05. At what significance level is each pairwise test run?
options: About 0.0083
About 0.0167
ba-w4-q5.explanation: With 4 groups there are m = 4 × 3 / 2 = 6 pairs, so each test is at α / m = 0.05 / 6 ≈ 0.0083, option B. Trap: option A divides by the number of groups (4), not the number of pairs; option D assumes 3 comparisons; option C applies no correction at all.

ba-w4-q6.question: A supermarket chain (fictional) tested 3 shelf layouts in 12 stores (4 stores per layout). Weekly sales (₹ lakh) are shown below. What are the one-way ANOVA F and η², and what is the decision at 5% (F(2, 9) critical = 4.256)?
options: F ≈ 1.72, H₀ not rejected; η² ≈ 0.63
F ≈ 7.75, reject H₀; η² ≈ 1.72
F ≈ 15.5, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.63
F ≈ 7.75, reject H₀; η² ≈ 0.63
ba-w4-q6.explanation: Means 11.5, 14.5, 12; grand mean 12.667. SSB = 4 × (1.167² + 1.833² + 0.667²) ≈ 20.67. SSW = 5 + 5 + 2 = 12. MSB = 20.67 / 2 = 10.33, MSW = 12 / 9 = 1.333, F ≈ 7.75 > 4.256 ⇒ reject. η² = 20.67 / 32.67 ≈ 0.63, so option D. Trap: option C forgets to divide SSB by df = 2; option A treats SSB / SSW as F; option B uses that same ratio as η², but η² has SST in the denominator.
